title: Synthetic Fibres and Plastics
description: Grade 8 Science: natural vs synthetic fibres, types of synthetic fibres (rayon, nylon, polyester, acrylic), plastics, thermoplastics vs thermosetting, and plastic & the environment.

topics.title: Natural and Synthetic Fibres
topics.concept:
A fibre is a thin, thread-like strand from which yarn and fabrics are made. Based on their source, fibres are of two kinds.

  • Natural fibres are obtained from plants and animals — for example cotton and jute (from plants) and wool and silk (from animals).
  • Synthetic (man-made) fibres are made by human beings in factories from chemicals obtained mostly from petroleum (a substance called petrochemicals).

A synthetic fibre is made of very large numbers of small units joined together in a long chain. Each small unit is a monomer, and the long chain made of many monomers is a polymer (poly = many, mer = part). So a synthetic fibre is a polymer. Interestingly, many natural materials are polymers too — cotton is a polymer called cellulose.

Synthetic fibres have become very popular because they are usually strong, cheap, durable and easy to wash and dry, and they do not wrinkle easily. This is why they are widely used for clothing and many other products.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify these as natural or synthetic fibres: cotton, nylon, wool, polyester.
examples.solution:
Natural fibres come from plants/animals; synthetic ones are made in factories.

  • Natural: cotton (plant), wool (animal).
  • Synthetic: nylon, polyester.
examples.answer: Natural: cotton and wool. Synthetic: nylon and polyester.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is a polymer? How is it related to a monomer?
examples.solution:
Polymers are built from repeating units.

  • A monomer is a single small unit.
  • A polymer is a long chain made by joining many monomers together.
examples.answer: A polymer is a long chain made of many small repeating units called monomers joined together.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two reasons why synthetic fibres are widely used for clothing.
examples.solution:
Think about their useful properties.

  • They are strong, cheap and durable.
  • They are easy to wash, dry quickly and do not wrinkle much.
examples.answer: Because they are strong, cheap and durable, and they wash and dry easily without wrinkling.

recap:
• A fibre is a thread-like strand used to make fabrics.
  • Natural fibres come from plants/animals (cotton, jute, wool, silk); synthetic fibres are made in factories from petrochemicals.
  • A polymer is a long chain of many small repeating units called monomers; synthetic fibres are polymers.
  • Synthetic fibres are strong, cheap, durable and easy to wash and dry.

quiz.q: A long chain made of many small repeating units (monomers) is called a:
quiz.explanation: A polymer is a large molecule formed by joining many monomers.

quiz.q: Which of these is a synthetic fibre?
quiz.explanation: Nylon is man-made (synthetic); cotton, wool and jute are natural.

topics.title: Types of Synthetic Fibres
topics.concept:
There are several important synthetic fibres, each with its own properties and uses.

  • Rayon — made from wood pulp (a natural source), so it is a partly man-made fibre, also called artificial silk. It is cheap, has a silk-like shine, and is used for clothes and bedsheets.
  • Nylon — the first fully synthetic fibre, made without any natural raw material. It is very strong, elastic and light, and is used in socks, ropes, tents, parachutes, seat belts, toothbrush bristles and fishing nets. Nylon is so strong that a nylon thread can be stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness.
  • Polyester — made of repeating units of an ester. It does not crease (wrinkle) easily, so it stays neat and is ideal for dress material. A popular polyester is Terylene; PET (used to make plastic bottles) is also a polyester. Terycot and Terywool are made by mixing polyester with cotton or wool.
  • Acrylic — a synthetic fibre that resembles wool. Clothes such as sweaters and blankets made from acrylic are cheaper and more durable than those made from natural wool.

Fibres are often blended (mixed) — for example polyester with cotton (polycot) — to combine the good qualities of both.

examples.solution:
Rayon resembles silk but is made differently.

  • It is made from wood pulp, not from silkworms.
  • It is cheap and has a silk-like shine, so it is called artificial silk.
examples.answer: Because it is a man-made fibre (from wood pulp) that has a silk-like shine, so it imitates silk cheaply.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the synthetic fibre best suited for making parachutes and ropes, and give a reason.
examples.solution:
Choose the fibre by its strength.

  • Nylon is very strong, elastic and light.
  • So it is used for ropes, parachutes, tents and seat belts.
examples.answer: Nylon, because it is very strong, light and elastic.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is polyester a good choice for school uniforms and dress material?
examples.solution:
Think about its main property.

  • Polyester does not wrinkle (crease) easily.
  • So clothes stay neat and need little ironing.
examples.answer: Because polyester does not crease easily, so the clothes remain neat and need little ironing.

recap:
• Rayon (from wood pulp) = artificial silk; cheap and shiny.
  • Nylon = first fully synthetic fibre; very strong, elastic and light (ropes, parachutes).
  • Polyester = does not crease (Terylene, PET); good for dress material.
  • Acrylic resembles wool (sweaters, blankets); fibres are often blended (polycot).

quiz.q: Which synthetic fibre is made from wood pulp and is called artificial silk?
quiz.explanation: Rayon is made from wood pulp and resembles silk.

quiz.q: The synthetic fibre that resembles wool and is used in sweaters is:
quiz.explanation: Acrylic resembles wool and is used for sweaters and blankets.

topics.title: Plastics and the Environment
topics.concept:
Plastic is also a polymer, like synthetic fibre. In some plastics the units are arranged in a straight line; in others they are joined in a cross-linked (網-like) pattern. Based on how they behave on heating, plastics are of two kinds.

  • Thermoplastics — plastics that soften on heating and can be bent and remoulded again and again. Examples: polythene (used in bags) and PVC (used in pipes, toys, bottles).
  • Thermosetting plastics — plastics that, once moulded by heat, cannot be softened or remoulded. Examples: bakelite (used in electric switches and handles of utensils because it is a poor conductor of heat and electricity) and melamine (used for floor tiles and unbreakable crockery).

Plastic is useful because it is light, strong, durable, cheap, a poor conductor of heat and electricity, and does not react with air, water or many chemicals (so it does not rust). This is why it is used for buckets, bottles, packaging, insulation of wires and even in cars and aeroplanes.

But plastic causes a serious problem: it is non-biodegradable — it is not broken down by natural processes, so it stays in the environment for a very long time, polluting land and water and harming animals that swallow it. We should follow the 4 R’s — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Recover — and avoid single-use plastic to protect the environment.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is bakelite used for the handles of electrical switches and frying pans?
examples.solution:
Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic with special properties.

  • It is a poor conductor of heat and electricity.
  • So it keeps us safe from electric shock and from getting burnt.
examples.answer: Because bakelite is a poor conductor of heat and electricity, making switches and handles safe to touch.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give one difference between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.
examples.solution:
Compare how they behave on heating.

  • Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded.
  • Thermosetting plastics, once set, cannot be softened or remoulded.
examples.answer: Thermoplastics soften and can be remoulded on heating, while thermosetting plastics cannot be softened or remoulded once set.

examples.problem: Example 3: What does it mean to say that plastic is non-biodegradable, and why is this a problem?
examples.solution:
Biodegradable materials are broken down by nature.

  • Non-biodegradable means it is not broken down by natural processes.
  • So plastic remains in the environment for a very long time, polluting it and harming living things.
examples.answer: Non-biodegradable means natural processes cannot break it down, so plastic stays for years, polluting land and water and harming animals.

recap:
• Plastic is a polymer; thermoplastics (polythene, PVC) soften and remould on heating.
  • Thermosetting plastics (bakelite, melamine) cannot be remoulded; bakelite is a poor conductor used in switches.
  • Plastic is light, strong, cheap, unreactive and a poor conductor — but non-biodegradable.
  • Follow the 4 R’s (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover) and avoid single-use plastic.

quiz.q: Plastics that soften on heating and can be remoulded again and again are:
quiz.explanation: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded.

quiz.q: Plastic harms the environment mainly because it is:
quiz.explanation: Plastic is non-biodegradable, so it stays in the environment for a very long time.

questions.q: A thin, thread-like strand used to make fabrics is a:
questions.explanation: A fibre is a thread-like strand from which fabrics are made.

questions.q: Which of these is a natural fibre?
questions.explanation: Cotton is obtained from a plant, so it is a natural fibre.

questions.q: Synthetic fibres are mostly made from chemicals obtained from:
questions.explanation: Synthetic fibres are made from petrochemicals obtained from petroleum.

questions.q: The single small unit that joins to form a polymer is a:
questions.explanation: Monomers join together to form a polymer.

questions.q: A polymer is a:
questions.explanation: A polymer is a large molecule made of many repeating monomer units.

questions.q: Rayon is made from:
questions.explanation: Rayon is made from wood pulp and is called artificial silk.

questions.q: The first fully synthetic fibre, very strong and used in parachutes, is:
questions.explanation: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fibre; it is strong and used in parachutes and ropes.

questions.q: Which synthetic fibre does NOT crease easily and is good for dress material?
questions.explanation: Polyester does not wrinkle easily, so it is ideal for clothes.

questions.q: The synthetic fibre that resembles wool is:
questions.explanation: Acrylic resembles wool and is used for sweaters and blankets.

questions.q: PET, used to make plastic bottles, is a type of:
questions.explanation: PET is a polyester used for bottles and containers.

questions.q: Plastics that soften on heating and can be remoulded are called:
questions.explanation: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded (e.g. polythene, PVC).

questions.q: Bakelite and melamine are examples of:
questions.explanation: Bakelite and melamine are thermosetting plastics that cannot be remoulded.

questions.q: Bakelite is used for electrical switches because it is a:
options: Poor conductor of heat and electricity
questions.explanation: Bakelite is a poor conductor of heat and electricity, making switches safe.

questions.q: A major environmental problem with plastic is that it is:
questions.explanation: Plastic is non-biodegradable, so it stays in the environment for a long time.

questions.q: Which set of actions helps reduce plastic pollution?
questions.explanation: The 4 R's — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover — help cut plastic pollution.

questions.q: A nylon thread can be stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness. This makes nylon especially suitable for:
questions.explanation: Nylon's great strength suits ropes, parachutes and seat belts.

questions.q: Terycot is made by mixing two fibres. They are:
questions.explanation: Terycot is a blend of polyester (Terylene) and cotton, combining their qualities.

questions.q: Why are the handles of cooking utensils often made of thermosetting plastic rather than metal?
options: The plastic is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays cool
questions.explanation: Thermosetting plastics like bakelite are poor heat conductors, so handles do not get hot.

questions.q: Firefighters' suits are sometimes coated with melamine because melamine:
questions.explanation: Melamine resists fire and heat, so it is used on firefighters' uniforms.

questions.q: Synthetic clothes can be dangerous near a flame because they:
options: Melt and stick to the skin
questions.explanation: Synthetic fibres melt and can stick to the body, which is why cotton is safer near fire.

questions.q: Why is it better to carry a cloth or jute bag instead of a plastic bag?
options: Cloth and jute are biodegradable and reusable
questions.explanation: Cloth and jute are natural, biodegradable and reusable, reducing plastic waste.
